Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne’er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman’s hallo’, Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins’ russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor’s sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more agèd, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney’s box, Must soon partake his grave.

**Epitaph on a Hare**

Here lies one whom no hound did e’er pursue,
Nor swifter greyhound follow,
Whose foot ne’er tainted the morning dew,
Nor ear e’er heard the huntsman’s hallo—

Old Tiney, surliest of his kind,
Who, nursed with tender care,
And to domestic bounds confined,
Was yet a wild jack-hare.

Though duly, from my hand, each night
His pittance he would take,
He did it with a jealous look,
And, given cause, would bite.

His diet was of wheaten bread,
Of milk, and oats, and straw,
Of thistles, or of lettuce fed,
With sand to scour his maw.

On twigs of hawthorn he regaled,
On pippins’ russet peel;
And when his juicy salads failed,
Sliced carrot pleased him well.

A Turkey carpet was his lawn,
Whereon he loved to bound,
To skip and gambol like a fawn,
And swing his haunches round.

His frisking hour was eventide,
For then he lost his fear;
But most before the showers would ride,
Or when a storm drew near.

Eight years and five round-rolling moons
He thus beheld steal away,
Dozing away his idle noons,
And every night at play.

I kept him for his humor’s sake,
For oft he would beguile
My heart of thoughts that made it ache,
And force upon me a smile.

But now, beneath this walnut-shade,
He finds his long, last home,
And waits, in snug concealment laid,
Till gentler Puss shall come.

He, still more aged, feels the shocks
From which no care can save,
And, partner once of Tiney’s box,
Must soon partake his grave.
outputs.L2:
Buried in this spot rests a creature that no hunting dog ever chased, that no fast greyhound ever ran after. His paws never left prints in the fresh morning dew, and he never heard a hunter's shout. This was old Tiney, the most bad-tempered of all his kind. Even though he'd been raised gently and kept within the limits of a home, he remained a wild male hare at heart.

Every evening I fed him from my own hand, and he always accepted his small portion. Yet he took it warily, watching me with distrust, and given the chance, he'd sink his teeth into me.

His meals consisted of bread made from wheat, along with milk, oats, and straw. Sometimes he ate thistles or lettuce instead, and he used sand to clean out his stomach. He nibbled on hawthorn branches and the reddish-brown skins of apples. Whenever fresh, moist greens ran out, he happily settled for slices of carrot.

A Turkish rug served as his meadow, and he delighted in leaping across it. He would hop and frolic just like a young deer, twisting his backside about as he played. His playful moods came in the evening, when his nervousness melted away, though he was liveliest just before rain arrived or when a storm was building.

For eight full years and five turning months, he watched time slip quietly by, sleeping through his lazy afternoons and playing every night. I kept him around because of his temperament, for he would often distract me from painful thoughts and coax a smile out of me.

Now, though, he rests forever beneath this walnut tree. He lies hidden away in comfort, waiting for the day when kinder Puss will join him. Puss, who is even older, suffers troubles that no amount of care can prevent. Once he shared Tiney's enclosure, and soon enough he'll share his grave as well.
outputs.L3:
# Old Tiney

Old Tiney was a wild jack-hare, and though he had been domesticated and raised with the most tender care, he never truly surrendered his untamed and surly nature. From the very beginning, something wild remained in him—a spirit that no amount of gentle handling could soften or subdue.

Every night, faithfully, I fed him, yet he never came to trust me. Despite the years we spent together and the care I lavished upon him, Tiney remained ever suspicious, and he would seize any opportunity to bite the hand that offered him nourishment. Such was his stubborn and independent character.

For all his surliness, Tiney thrived under my roof. He flourished on a varied diet of bread and milk, oats, fresh vegetables, and the peels of fruit. And though he distrusted me, he took great delight in frisking and playing about, most especially before an approaching storm, when some restless energy seemed to seize him and set him leaping with peculiar joy.

Tiney lived a long life for a creature of his kind—eight years and five months in all. When at last he died, I buried him beneath the walnut tree, laying to rest a companion who, for all his faults, had been dear to me.

For I cherished old Tiney more than his temperament might suggest. In his own strange way, he had the power to lift my spirits and to ease my aching heart in times of sorrow. Now, with him gone, I find myself turning to my other hare, Puss, who is likewise growing old—and I cannot help but anticipate, with quiet melancholy, the day when I must part with her as well.

# Old Tiney: An Elegy

For eight long years, Old Tiney shared my home, though never once did he surrender the untamed spirit that ran in his blood. A jack-hare by nature—surliest of his kind—he remained perpetually wild despite the comfort and care I lavished upon him. No amount of gentleness could fully domesticate the wariness in his eyes, nor coax from him the easy trust that other creatures might have offered. And yet, in his own guarded way, he became a companion whose loss I now mourn deeply.

I came to know his habits as one knows an old friend. I learned the particular foods he favored—the tender lettuce leaves, the sweet carrots, the sprigs of parsley that he would nibble with such deliberate care. I observed how he would tuck himself away during the long hours of daylight, cautious and reserved, keeping to the shadows as if some ancient instinct warned him against the openness of day.

But it was in the evenings that Tiney truly came alive. When the household settled into quiet and the lamps were lit, he would emerge from his reserve and give himself over to play. Round and round the room he would circle, describing wild and joyful loops across the floor, his feet drumming a merry rhythm as he leaped and turned. In those moments, all his daytime caution fell away, and he became a creature of pure, exuberant motion—a small marvel of life bounding through my quiet rooms.

These antics, trivial as they might seem to others, meant more to me than words can easily express. For I have carried a heavy heart through many difficult seasons, and my spirits have often sunk beneath burdens I could not lift alone. It was then that Tiney served his greatest purpose. To watch his innocent frolic, to smile at his harmless games, was to feel some portion of my sorrow lighten. He drew me, however briefly, out of my melancholy and gave me cause to laugh when laughter seemed impossible. In easing my aching heart, this wild little creature performed a kindness he could never have understood.

Now Tiney is gone, and I set down this tribute in his memory. Yet even as I grieve, my thoughts turn with tenderness—and no small dread—toward Puss, my other companion, who grows old and frail before my eyes. I know that his death, too, cannot be far off, and the anticipation of that coming loss deepens the sorrow of this present one. Together these small companions have been my solace; to lose them is to lose the gentle comforts that made my heavy days more bearable.

Rest now, Old Tiney, surly and wild to the last, but dearer to me than you ever knew.

# The Quiet Ownership of Place

**Here** is where every journey eventually leads us back. No matter how far we wander, there remains a single point on the map that feels like home—a place that anchors us when everything else drifts.

But belonging is a complicated thing. It cannot be bought, **nor** can it be forced. You may live somewhere for years and still feel like a stranger, while another person might arrive and instantly feel they have found their true place in the world. Belonging is neither about the length of time we spend somewhere, **nor** about the papers that declare our residence official.

The real question is one of connection. **Whose** memories fill these streets? **Whose** hands built the walls that shelter us, and **whose** stories echo in the rooms where we sleep? A house becomes a home only when we can answer these questions—when the space around us carries the weight of shared history and personal meaning.

Consider the traveler who stands at a crossroads, uncertain which path to take. **Here**, at this moment of decision, they must ask themselves what they truly seek. Comfort cannot come from location alone, **nor** from possessions, **nor** from the approval of others. It comes from within, from knowing **whose** voice matters most: your own.

In the end, we each build our own sense of *here*. We decide **whose** opinions we value and **whose** we release. We accept that peace comes neither from running away **nor** from standing perfectly still, but from finally understanding where—and to whom—we truly belong.
